prompt.context: You are an inventor whose most recent creation is a new type of golf ball. The golf ball is indestructible and cannot be lost.
prompt.question: What should the price of the golf ball be?

clarifying_info.q: Do I need to build up my own assumptions?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, you are required to generate all assumptions on your own.

clarifying_info.q: Should I account for the time value of money?
clarifying_info.a: Don't worry about the time value of money.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the ball cost to produce?
clarifying_info.a: The golf ball costs $200 to produce.

clarifying_info.q: Are there fixed costs or R&D costs to consider?
clarifying_info.a: No fixed costs or R&D costs for now.

framework: Determine the price floor: cost to produce the ball ($200)
Determine the price ceiling: lifetime savings of the average golfer compared to buying regular golf balls
Calculate lifetime ball usage: rounds per year x balls per round x years of play
Estimate cost of regular balls over a lifetime to derive maximum willingness to pay
Set price between floor and ceiling, adjusting for age/segment differences
Consider financing mechanisms for younger or cash-constrained golfers
Identify the structural market problem: one-time purchase collapses recurring demand

questions.prompt: What is the price floor for the Amazing Golf Ball?
questions.guidance: The price floor is the production cost. The interviewer confirms it is $200 per ball with no fixed or R&D costs to consider for now.

math.setup: Price floor = variable cost per unit

questions.prompt: Calculate the lifetime savings of an average golfer if they use the Amazing Golf Ball instead of regular balls.
questions.guidance: Candidate must build up assumptions for: (1) frequency of play, (2) balls used per round, (3) cost per regular ball, (4) years of play. Multiply to get total lifetime spend on regular balls, which sets the price ceiling.

math.setup: Lifetime balls used = rounds/year x balls/round x years played; Lifetime spend = lifetime balls x cost per ball
steps: Rounds per month: 2; balls per round: 3 → 6 balls/month = 72 balls/year ≈ 70 balls/year
Average golfer starts at age 35, lives to 70 → plays 35 years
Lifetime spend on regular balls: 2,500 x $2 = $5,000
math.answer: Price ceiling = $5,000 (maximum willingness to pay for a golfer starting at age 35)

questions.prompt: Given the floor and ceiling, what exact price would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should narrow the range with reasoning. A rational customer who plays for 35 years would pay up to $5,000, but real-world friction (uncertainty about future play, large upfront outlay, older golfers with fewer years remaining) pulls the optimal price down. The example dialogue suggests ~$2,000 as a defensible midpoint. Candidate should acknowledge market research is needed but commit to a number.

math.setup: Suggested price = midpoint adjusted for real-world willingness to pay
steps: Discount for uncertainty, consumer psychology, and age mix of buyers

questions.prompt: How would you handle pricing for different age segments (e.g., older golfers with fewer remaining years, or young golfers with limited cash)?
questions.guidance: Strong answers address: (1) senior discount since older golfers have fewer years of savings remaining; (2) financing/installment plan for young golfers who lack upfront cash but have the longest playing horizon (50+ years of savings). The student-loan analogy — small down payment plus principal and interest over time — is the model answer.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental market problem with this product, and how would you address investor concerns?
questions.guidance: Once every golfer owns a ball, demand collapses to population growth only (and even that is offset by inheritance). Investors put in capital today for a one-time market. The pitch to investors: the first-year revenue opportunity is enormous (60 million golfers x ~$2,000 price vs. $200 cost = ~$108B revenue, ~$10.8B cost, ~$97B profit). Investors can extract their return within a year and redeploy capital elsewhere — framing it as a high-return, short-duration investment.

math.setup: Total first-year revenue and profit opportunity
steps: 60 million golfers x $2,000 price = $120 billion revenue
60 million golfers x $200 cost = $12 billion cost
math.answer: ~$108 billion gross profit in year 1; investors should treat it as a high-return one-shot opportunity and exit after year 1

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the strategic and market considerations relevant to pricing and selling the Amazing Golf Ball?

categories.name: Pricing Framework
ideas: Set floor at production cost ($200)
Set ceiling at customer lifetime value (savings on regular balls = $5,000)
Adjust for age-based willingness to pay
Adjust for uncertainty about future golf play
Consider psychological price anchors

categories.name: Segmentation & Discounting
ideas: Senior discount for golfers with fewer remaining years
Youth/student financing plan (low upfront, installment payments)
Market research to determine exact price point by segment

categories.name: Financing Mechanisms
ideas: Installment payments similar to student loans
Small down payment with principal and interest over time
Subscription or leasing model

categories.name: Market Structure Problem
ideas: One-time purchase market: no repeat customers once everyone owns a ball
Future demand limited to population growth
Ball can be inherited, further suppressing replacement demand
Must generate all returns in initial sales wave

categories.name: Investor Pitch
ideas: Frame as a high-return, short-duration opportunity
Quantify the one-year gross profit opportunity
Emphasize investors can exit and redeploy after year 1

categories.name: Competitive & Operational
ideas: No competitors with equivalent product
Production cost is known ($200); margin is controllable
Distribution channel selection (golf stores, direct, online)

recommendation: Price the Amazing Golf Ball at approximately $2,000, which is well below the average golfer's lifetime spend on regular balls ($5,000) but well above production cost ($200)

Implement age-based segmentation: senior discount for older golfers with fewer remaining years, and an installment financing plan for younger golfers who lack upfront cash but have the highest lifetime savings potential
risks: The market is structurally a one-time opportunity — once saturation is reached, demand collapses to near zero
Consumer resistance to a $2,000 golf ball may be high; actual willingness to pay requires market research
Older golfers' willingness to pay is significantly lower than the $5,000 ceiling; blended pricing needed
next_steps: Conduct market research to validate price sensitivity across age segments
Model financing terms for youth buyers to ensure adequate returns
Develop investor materials framing this as a high-return one-shot investment with rapid capital recovery
